transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I came in because lately, since I started helping with the safety trainings at work, I can’t stop noticing my hands. When I’m pointing things out, they look so wrinkly and uneven to me. And then I’ll see myself in the newsletter photos and start thinking my face looks crooked, even though other people say they don’t really see it. It’s been bothering me enough that I thought I should talk to someone.
How much time do you spend each day thinking about the way your hands or face look, and does it interfere with your daily activities or cause you significant distress?

It’s hard to say exactly, but it’s been happening pretty often. Since I started helping with the safety trainings, I keep noticing my hands when I’m pointing at things—they look wrinkly and uneven to me. Then if I see a newsletter photo, I get stuck thinking my face looks crooked, even when people tell me they don’t see it. It does bother me and distracts me more than I’d like.
Do you find yourself worrying about other parts of your body besides your hands and face, or is it mostly those areas that concern you?

Mostly those areas, my hands and my face. The hands stand out when I’m pointing during the safety trainings, and then the face thing comes up when I see those newsletter photos. I haven’t really been worrying about other body parts the same way.
When you’re worried about the way your hands or face look, do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking mirrors, taking photos, or trying to fix them in some way?

Yes. Before a class or one of the senior-center workshops, I’ll usually check the bathroom mirror a few times. I’ll put lotion on my hands, look at my face from different angles, that kind of thing. Sometimes I ask a coworker if I look all right. It can make me run a little late, but I still get myself there.
Do you believe that the wrinkles on your hands or the crookedness of your face are defects or flaws that make you look unattractive or abnormal?

Yes… I guess I do see them that way. When I’m pointing things out in the safety trainings, my hands look really wrinkly and uneven to me, like it’s obvious. And with my face, especially in the newsletter photos, I keep thinking it looks crooked, even though other people say they don’t see it. It makes me feel like I look unattractive or not normal.
When you look at your hands or face and notice the wrinkles or the crookedness, do you think other people are noticing them the same way you do, or do you feel like they don’t see it the way you do?

I think I notice it more than other people do. Like with my hands, when I’m pointing during the safety trainings, I can’t stop seeing how wrinkly and uneven they look. And with my face in the newsletter photos, I think it looks crooked, but people tell me they don’t really see it. So… I guess they don’t see it the way I do.
When you're thinking about your hands or face looking wrinkled or crooked, does this lead you to feel anxious, depressed, or does it mostly make you feel self-conscious about your appearance?

Mostly it makes me really self-conscious. I came in because since I started helping with the safety trainings, I just can’t stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out. And then I start looking at the newsletter photos and thinking my face looks crooked, even though people tell me they don’t see it. It bothers me and I get stuck on it.
Because of how you feel about your hands or face, do you ever avoid doing things—like leading a training or appearing in photos—or try to hide those parts of your body from others?

It hasn’t made me stop working or helping with the trainings, no. But I do take longer getting ready now, making sure my hands don’t look so bad. And I’ve started trying to avoid being in photos when I can… or I’ll hesitate before going to social things that I used to just go to without thinking so much.

Have these concerns about your hands and face ever made it hard for you to function in your job, relationships, or other important areas of your life, such as avoiding events or interactions altogether?

It hasn’t really stopped me from doing my job or helping with the trainings. I still go. But it does slow me down getting ready, especially if I know I’ll be in front of people. And I’ve started ducking out of photos when I can, or hesitating before social things I used to just go to without thinking. So it affects me some, but I’m not avoiding everything altogether.
Do you worry about your weight or body shape in general, or are your concerns mostly limited to your hands and face looking wrinkled or crooked?

No, it’s not really about my weight or my overall body shape. It’s mostly my hands and my face. Since I started doing the safety trainings, I keep noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m pointing at things. And then with the newsletter photos, I start thinking my face looks crooked, even when other people say they don’t see it.
Do you feel like others are judging you negatively or thinking badly of you because of how your hands or face look?
I’m not really sure. I mean, I worry they might notice it, but I can’t say I know they’re judging me. Nobody’s said anything bad to me about it. It’s more something I get stuck thinking about myself.
Do you ever feel like the thoughts about your hands or face looking wrinkled or crooked come up so often or feel so intense that they’re hard to control, even when you try to focus on something else?

Yes, that’s pretty much why I came in. Since I started helping with the safety trainings, I can’t seem to stop noticing my hands, like how wrinkly or uneven they look when I’m pointing things out. And then with the newsletter photos, I’ll look at my face and start thinking it looks crooked, even though other people tell me they don’t see it. It’s hard to just drop it once it gets in my head.
Do these thoughts about your hands and face ever feel so overwhelming or consuming that you spend a lot of time thinking about them, even when you don’t want to?

Yes. It does get pretty consuming sometimes. That’s really why I came in. Since I started helping with the safety trainings, I keep noticing my hands when I’m pointing at things, thinking they look wrinkly or uneven. And then I’ll see my face in the newsletter photos and think it looks crooked, even when people tell me they don’t see it. I don’t want to keep thinking about it, but it kind of sticks.

Have these concerns about your hands or face ever caused problems with your ability to work, maintain relationships, or participate in social activities, beyond the hesitation or preparation time you’ve already mentioned?

It hasn’t really stopped me from doing things, no. I still go to work and I still help with the trainings. But I am slower getting ready for them, and I’ve started avoiding photos when I can. Sometimes before social things, I hesitate more than I used to, even if it’s something I would normally enjoy.
Do the thoughts about your hands and face ever take up so much of your time or feel so important that you have trouble focusing on anything else, even for a little while?

Yes, at times. That’s kind of what pushed me to come in. When I’m doing the safety trainings, I notice my hands while I’m pointing, and then I get stuck thinking they look wrinkly or uneven. And with the newsletter photos, I’ll start focusing on my face looking crooked, even though people say they don’t see it. It can make it hard to pay attention to anything else for a bit.

Do you feel like your concerns about your hands or face looking wrinkled or crooked take up so much of your time or attention that it feels hard to manage your day, or that it significantly affects how you feel about yourself?

Yes, it does affect how I feel about myself. I came in because since I started helping with the safety trainings, I keep noticing my hands when I’m pointing things out, like they look wrinkly or uneven. Then with the newsletter photos, I start thinking my face looks crooked, even though other people say they don’t see it. I know I’ve said that, but it’s like I can’t quite stop noticing it.
